title: What Happens When You Type a URL

cards.prompt:
You type `https://www.example.com/news` and press **Enter**. Less than a second later, the page is on your screen, and almost everything in this course has happened.

First, your [[browser]] reads the address, called a **URL**. Match each part to what the browser does with it.

pairs.right: Encrypt everything with TLS, on port 443
Turn it into an IP address with DNS
Ask the server for that page with GET

cards.explanation: The first part, the **scheme**, picks the [[protocol]]: `https` means HTTP inside TLS. The **host** is the name DNS turns into an address. The **path** goes into the GET request, so the server knows which page you want.
cards.hint: One part picks the protocol, one is a name that needs looking up, and one says which page.
cards.nudge: Names have to become numbers before anything can connect. And the part after the slash is the same kind of thing you saw in `GET /news`.

cards.prompt: **Step 1: [[DNS]].** The [[browser]] needs an [[IP address]] for `www.example.com`. Do the lookup yourself with `nslookup www.example.com`.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of www.example.com
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
www.example.com	canonical name = example.com.
Name:	example.com
Address: 198.51.100.10
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

success.question: Which IPv4 address will the browser connect to?

cards.explanation: The answer is `198.51.100.10`. The `canonical name` line is a CNAME: `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com`, so these are example.com's addresses. The name also has an [[IPv6]] address, `2001:db8::10`, and many browsers try that first. Either way, the lookup probably came from a [[cache]], or a [[resolver]] asked the root, `.com` and example.com's own servers, all in a few milliseconds.
cards.hint: The `Server` lines at the top are the helper that answered. Look further down, under the answer, for the website's address.
cards.nudge: The top `Address` line is the DNS helper, not the website. Look below `Non-authoritative answer`, and pick the one written with dots, not colons.

cards.prompt: **Step 2: the first [[packet]] leaves.** It's the first message of TCP's [[handshake]] ("Can we talk?"), addressed to `198.51.100.10:443`. Send it from the laptop to the web [[server]]. (The home [[router]] shows its **public** address, the one the internet sees.)
cards.explanation: Either ISP router works: each router just picks a good next [[hop]]. On the way out, the home router used **NAT** to swap the laptop's private `192.168.1.20` for its own public `203.0.113.7`, and noted who asked. That public address is the only one the server ever sees.
cards.hint: Every packet from home has to leave through the home router first. After that, follow any links that lead to the server.
cards.nudge: Devices at home can't reach the internet directly: their packets go through the home router. The Smart TV isn't on the way.

cards.prompt: **Steps 1 to 4 in one go.** `curl -v` fetches a page and shows each step as it happens. Run `curl -v https://www.example.com/news` and watch the lookup, the connection, the TLS [[handshake]] and the request go by. Which **port** did it connect to?

success.question: Which port did curl connect to?

cards.explanation: `Connected to www.example.com (198.51.100.10) port 443`: port **443**, the [[HTTPS]] port. Reading from the top, you can see the whole course: the **DNS** answer, the **TCP** connection (`Connected`), the **TLS** handshake and [[certificate]] check, the [[encrypted|encryption]] request (`GET /news`) and the reply (`200`). (curl tried the IPv6 address first, but this network has no IPv6, so it used [[IPv4]].)
cards.hint: Find the line that starts `Connected to`. The port is at the end of that line.
cards.nudge: The first `Trying` line failed. Look for the line that says `Connected to` and read the number after `port`.

cards.title: Rebuilding the page
cards.body:
The reply comes back as **packets**, [[hop]] by hop, to your router's [[public address]]. **NAT** passes them to your laptop. **TCP** uses their [[sequence numbers|sequence-number]] to put them back in order, and asks again for any that got lost. **TLS** decrypts them.

Then your [[browser]] reads the [[HTML]], requests the pictures it mentions, and draws the page.

cards.prompt: Put the whole journey in order, from pressing Enter to seeing the page.

items.label: TCP handshake with the server on port 443
TLS handshake: keys agreed and the certificate checked
The browser sends an encrypted GET request for /news
The server replies with 200 OK and the page's HTML
TCP puts the packets back in order and TLS decrypts them
The browser fetches the pictures, then draws the page

cards.explanation: Find the address (**DNS**), open a reliable connection (**TCP**), secure it (**TLS**), ask (**GET**), get the answer (**200 OK**), rebuild and decrypt it, then draw it. Every one of these messages travelled as **packets**, [[hop]] by hop, through your [[router]]'s **NAT**, as **bits**.
cards.hint: You need an address before you can connect, a connection before you can secure it, and a secure connection before you ask for the page.
cards.nudge: Think about what each step needs first. You can't connect without an address, and you can't draw the page until it has arrived and been decrypted.

cards.prompt: When a page won't load, the error tells you which step failed. Match each error to the step.

pairs.right: The server has no page at that path

cards.explanation: **Server not found** means DNS couldn't turn the name into an address. **Timed out** means "Can we talk?" never got a reply. **Not private** is a failed certificate check in the TLS handshake. And **404** means everything worked right up to [[HTTP]], but there's nothing at that path.
cards.hint: Each error comes from a different step: finding the address, opening the connection, checking the certificate, or asking for the page.
cards.nudge: Read each error's words closely: the name can't be found, nothing answers, it's not private, or there's nothing at that path.

cards.prompt: Now the **reply**. The [[server]] sends the page to `203.0.113.7`, your home [[router]]'s [[public address]]. **Router A is down.** Route the reply back to the laptop that asked for it.
cards.explanation: With Router A down, the reply goes **B → C → home router**, a longer route than the request may have taken. That's fine: routes don't have to match in both directions. At the home router, **NAT** checks its notes of who asked and passes the reply to the laptop, not the phone.
cards.hint: A router that's down can't pass anything on, so find another way round. At the home router, only the device that asked should get the reply.
cards.nudge: Avoid any router that's down. And at the home router, NAT remembers which device made the request.

cards.title: Recap: How the Internet Works
cards.body:
- **DNS** finds the address; **packets** travel router to router.
- **TCP** connects reliably, **TLS** encrypts, **HTTP** asks and answers.
- It's all **bits**, going out and back through your router's **NAT**.

Take the final quiz to finish the course. Next time a page loads, you'll know what just happened.
